content: Moxibustion is a therapeutic practice rooted in traditional oriental medicine that involves the use of moxa, a preparation derived from the mugwort herb. This technique is integral to the medical traditions of China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Tibet, and Mongolia. The mugwort is typically aged and ground into a fine, fluffy substance, which is then either burned directly or processed into a stick resembling a cigar (though it is not intended for smoking). Practitioners may apply moxa indirectly, in conjunction with acupuncture needles, or occasionally burn it directly on the skin. The term moxa originates from the Japanese word mogusa (艾), where the u is softly pronounced. In Japan, the herb is also referred to as yomogi (蓬). In Chinese, the same character is used but pronounced as ài, and the processed form is called ài róng (艾絨), meaning velvet of ài. The Chinese character for moxa forms part of the term zhēn jiǔ (針灸), which is often translated as acupuncture. Moxibustion is employed to warm specific regions and acupuncture points, aiming to stimulate circulation and promote the smooth flow of blood and qi (vital energy). Research, such as that documented in the Encyclopedia of Alternative Medicine, has demonstrated that mugwort acts as an emmenagogue, stimulating blood flow in the pelvic region and uterus. It is also believed to counteract cold and dampness within the body and has been used to assist in turning breech presentations during pregnancy. Historical evidence suggests that moxibustion predates acupuncture, with the latter emerging as a complementary practice after the 2nd century BCE. Different schools of acupuncture incorporate moxibustion to varying extents. For instance, practitioners of the Five-Element acupuncture tradition may apply moxa directly to the skin, while those following Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) methods often use moxa rolls held above the treatment point. To prevent scarring, moxa can also be burned atop a thin slice of ginger root. Moxibustion is particularly valued for treating chronic conditions, deficient states (weakness), and age-related health issues. The semi-legendary Chinese physician Bian Que (circa 500 BCE), renowned as the first specialist in moxibustion, extolled its benefits over acupuncture in his classical writings. He argued that moxibustion could replenish energy in the body and address both excess and deficient conditions. Conversely, he cautioned against using acupuncture on patients with significant deficiencies, as needle manipulation could deplete their energy further. A notable classical text, the Gao Huang Shu (膏肓俞), focuses exclusively on the indications for moxibustion at a single acupuncture point. Additionally, Taoist practitioners have historically combined scarring moxibustion with Chinese medical astrology to promote longevity. Practitioners may also use acupuncture needles made from various materials in conjunction with moxa, depending on the desired direction of qi flow stimulation. In parallel traditions, mugwort has been revered by indigenous peoples in North and South America as a sacred plant for divination, spiritual healing, and as a general remedy. It was often incorporated into smudge sticks alongside other herbs. In Europe, mugwort was placed under pillows to induce vivid dreams and was associated with magical practices during Anglo-Saxon times.
